lessons.title: The Five Pillars, Shahadah and Salah

before.content_html:
The Five Pillars of Sunni Islam

Islam is built on five core duties known as the Five Pillars. Just as the pillars of a building hold up its roof, these five duties hold up the entire faith. If a Muslim neglects any one of them, their spiritual life is weakened. The Prophet Muhammad said: “Islam is built upon five things” (Hadith, Sahih al-Bukhari).

Key Fact

The Five Pillars are: Shahadah (declaration of faith), Salah (prayer five times daily), Zakah (charitable giving of 2.5% of savings), Sawm (fasting during Ramadan), and Hajj (pilgrimage to Makkah at least once in a lifetime).

The Five Pillars are not optional — they are fard (compulsory) for every adult Muslim of sound mind. They give Muslims a shared identity across the world, uniting the global ummah through common acts of worship, charity and devotion. Whether a Muslim lives in London, Jakarta or Cairo, these duties connect them to every other believer.

Each pillar addresses a different aspect of devotion. The Shahadah establishes belief, Salah maintains daily contact with God, Zakah ensures social responsibility, Sawm builds spiritual discipline, and Hajj connects Muslims to the origins of their faith. Together they form a complete framework for living according to Allah’s will. Neglecting any pillar is considered sinful because each one supports the others.

The Ten Obligatory Acts in Shi’a Islam

Shi’a Muslims — particularly Twelver Shi’a — follow the Ten Obligatory Acts. These include all of the Five Pillars (Salah, Sawm, Zakah, Hajj and Jihad) plus five additional duties that reflect Shi’a theological priorities.

The ten duties are: Salah (prayer), Sawm (fasting), Zakah (almsgiving), Hajj (pilgrimage), Khums (a 20% tax on surplus income), Jihad (striving in the way of God), Amr bil ma’ruf (commanding what is good), Nahi anil munkar (forbidding what is evil), Tawalla (loving the Ahl al-Bayt — the Prophet’s family), and Tabarra (dissociating from the enemies of the Ahl al-Bayt).

The additional duties reflect Shi’a emphasis on social justice, the authority of the Prophet’s family, and the responsibility of every Muslim to actively promote good and resist evil in society. Khums is particularly important because the money is partly given to the descendants of Muhammad, supporting the religious scholars who guide the Shi’a community.

Key Fact

Both Sunni and Shi’a Muslims share the core duties of prayer, fasting, charity and pilgrimage. The key difference is that Shi’a Muslims have additional obligations including Khums (20% tax) and duties related to social justice and loyalty to the Prophet’s family.

The Shahadah — Declaration of Faith

The Shahadah is the first and most fundamental of the Five Pillars. It is a single sentence that captures the entire foundation of Muslim belief:

Key Fact

“La ilaha illa Allah wa-Muhammad rasul Allah” — “There is no God but Allah and Muhammad is the Prophet of Allah.”

The first half of the Shahadah affirms Tawhid — the oneness of God. This rejects any form of Shirk (associating anything with God). The second half acknowledges Muhammad as God’s final messenger, meaning Muslims accept the authority of his teachings and the Qur’an.

The Shahadah in Daily Life

The Shahadah is woven into every stage of a Muslim’s life. It is whispered into the ear of a newborn baby so it is the first thing the child hears. It is recited during every set of daily prayers. Muslims hope it will be the last words they speak before death. Sincerely reciting the Shahadah before Muslim witnesses is the only requirement for converting to Islam — once spoken with genuine belief, a person becomes part of the ummah.

Shi’a Muslims add a third clause to the Shahadah: “and Ali is the friend of God.” This reflects their belief that Ali, the Prophet’s cousin and son-in-law, was divinely appointed as Muhammad’s successor. By including Ali in the declaration of faith, Shi’a Muslims affirm the authority of the Imamate — the line of twelve Imams descended from Ali who they believe are the rightful leaders of Islam.

Why is the Shahadah the Most Important Pillar?

The Shahadah is placed first among the Five Pillars because it is the foundation for everything else. Without sincere belief in one God and the prophethood of Muhammad, the other pillars — prayer, charity, fasting and pilgrimage — would have no meaning. The Qur’an declares: “Your God is one God. There is no deity except Him, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful” (Qur’an 2:163). Every act of Islamic worship flows from this declaration.

Tawhid is not just a belief — it shapes every aspect of a Muslim’s life. If Allah is the only God, then only He deserves worship, obedience and devotion. This means Muslims should not place anything — money, status, other people — above God. Surah 112 states: “He is Allah, the One, Allah is Eternal and Absolute. None is born of Him, He is unborn. There is none like unto Him.” The Shahadah is how Muslims publicly commit themselves to this belief every single day.

glossary_terms.definition: The five essential religious duties that every Sunni Muslim must fulfil: Shahadah, Salah, Zakah, Sawm and Hajj.
A compulsory religious duty that all Muslims must perform as part of their submission to Allah.
The worldwide community of Muslims, bound together by shared faith and practice.
The largest branch of Shi’a Islam, whose followers believe in a line of twelve divinely appointed Imams descended from Ali.
Ten compulsory duties in Shi’a Islam that include the Five Pillars plus additional obligations such as Khums, Jihad and commanding good.
The Islamic declaration of faith: ‘There is no God but Allah and Muhammad is the Prophet of Allah.’
The belief in the absolute oneness of Allah — the most important concept in Islam.
The sin of associating partners with Allah or worshipping anything other than God — considered the greatest sin in Islam.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is NOT one of the Five Pillars of Islam?
A) Shahadah
B) Khums
C) Hajj
D) Sawm
practice_questions.marks: B — Khums. Khums is one of the Ten Obligatory Acts in Shi’a Islam, not one of the Five Pillars. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Give two of the Ten Obligatory Acts that are not part of the Five Pillars.
practice_questions.marks: Any two from: Khums / Amr bil ma’ruf (commanding good) / Nahi anil munkar (forbidding evil) / Tawalla (loving the Prophet’s family) / Tabarra (dissociating from enemies of the Prophet’s family). (1 mark for each, up to 2 marks)

practice_questions.text: Explain two similarities and/or differences between the Five Pillars of Sunni Islam and the Ten Obligatory Acts of Shi’a Islam.
practice_questions.marks:
Similarity: Both Sunni and Shi’a Muslims share core duties such as Salah (prayer), Sawm (fasting), Zakah (charity) and Hajj (pilgrimage). These practices unite the global Muslim community regardless of branch. (2 marks for developed point)
Difference: Shi’a Muslims follow additional obligations including Khums (a 20% tax on surplus income given partly to descendants of Muhammad) and duties related to social justice such as commanding good and forbidding evil. These reflect the Shi’a emphasis on the authority of the Prophet’s family. (2 marks for developed point)

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Shahadah is significant for Muslims. Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Way 1: The Shahadah affirms Tawhid — the belief that there is only one God. This is the most important concept in Islam because it means Muslims must worship Allah alone and reject Shirk. It shapes every aspect of daily life and worship. (1–2 marks)
Way 2: The Shahadah is recited throughout a Muslim’s life — whispered at birth, spoken during every prayer, and ideally the last words before death. Sincerely reciting it before witnesses is the only requirement for becoming a Muslim, making it the gateway to the entire faith. (1–2 marks)
Source: The Qur’an states ‘Your God is one God. There is no deity except Him’ (2:163), directly supporting the Tawhid expressed in the Shahadah. / Surah 112 declares Allah is ‘One, Eternal and Absolute.’ (1–2 marks)

practice_questions.text:
‘The Shahadah is the most important of the Five Pillars.’
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Muslim teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments for:
• The Shahadah is the first pillar and the foundation for all others — without sincere belief in God and Muhammad, the other pillars have no meaning.
• It is the only requirement for converting to Islam, showing it is the entry point to the entire faith.
• It affirms Tawhid, which the Qur’an calls the most fundamental belief (Surah 112).
• It is recited at birth, in every prayer, and at death — it defines a Muslim’s entire existence.

Arguments against:
• All five pillars are equally important because they work together like pillars supporting a building — removing any one weakens the whole.
• Salah is performed five times daily and is the most regular act of worship, creating constant awareness of God.
• Hajj requires enormous personal sacrifice and is described as ‘a duty owed to God by people’ (Qur’an 3:97).
• Zakah has a direct social impact, redistributing wealth and supporting the poor.

Top band (10–12) Well-argued response with developed points on both sides, religious references, and a justified conclusion.
Upper-mid band (7–9) Reasoned arguments on both sides with some development and references.
Lower-mid band (4–6) Reasoned arguments on one side or simple arguments on both sides.
Lower band (1–3) Simple statements or a single relevant point.

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between how Sunni and Shi’a Muslims recite the Shahadah.
practice_questions.marks:
Difference 1: Sunni Muslims recite ‘There is no God but Allah and Muhammad is the Prophet of Allah.’ This two-part declaration affirms Tawhid and the prophethood of Muhammad. (2 marks)
Difference 2: Shi’a Muslims add a third clause: ‘and Ali is the friend of God.’ This reflects their belief that Ali was divinely appointed as Muhammad’s successor, affirming the authority of the Imamate. (2 marks)

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes wudu?
A) A Friday sermon
B) A ritual washing before prayer
C) A type of fasting
D) A pilgrimage to Makkah
practice_questions.marks: B — A ritual washing before prayer. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Name two groups of people who are exempt from fasting during Ramadan.
practice_questions.marks: Any two from: young children / the elderly / pregnant women / breastfeeding women / people who are ill / travellers / those menstruating. (1 mark for each, up to 2 marks)

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between how Sunni and Shi’a Muslims perform Salah.
practice_questions.marks:
Difference 1: Sunni Muslims pray five separate times each day, treating each prayer as a distinct act of worship at its set time. Shi’a Muslims combine some prayers (Zuhr with Asr, Maghrib with Isha), so they pray in three sessions. (2 marks for developed point)
Difference 2: Shi’a Muslims may place a turbah (small clay tablet made from natural earth) on the ground to prostrate upon during prayer, as they believe the forehead should touch natural earth. Sunni Muslims prostrate directly onto the prayer mat or carpet. (2 marks for developed point)

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Sawm during Ramadan is important for Muslims. Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Reason 1: Sawm develops taqwa (God-consciousness) and self-discipline. By denying basic physical needs from dawn to sunset, Muslims strengthen their willpower and demonstrate obedience to Allah. This helps them resist temptation throughout the year. (1–2 marks)
Reason 2: Fasting creates empathy with the poor and hungry. By experiencing hunger first-hand, Muslims develop compassion and are motivated to give charity (Zakah). This strengthens social bonds within the ummah. (1–2 marks)
Source: The Qur’an states ‘It was in the month of Ramadan that the Qur’an was revealed as guidance for mankind. So any one of you who is present that month should fast’ (2:185), showing that fasting is a direct command from Allah linked to the revelation of His guidance. (1–2 marks)

practice_questions.text:
‘Praying in a mosque is always better than praying at home.’
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Muslim teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments for:
• Muhammad said prayer in congregation is ‘twenty-seven times more rewarding than prayer performed individually’ (Hadith), showing the Prophet valued mosque prayer.
• Mosque prayer strengthens the ummah by bringing Muslims together, creating a sense of community and shared worship.
• Jummah (Friday prayer) is compulsory in congregation — the Qur’an says ‘hurry towards the reminder of God’ (62:9).
• The imam’s leadership ensures prayers are performed correctly.

Arguments against:
• Islam teaches that the entire earth is a place of prayer — Muslims can pray anywhere that is clean, showing location is less important than sincerity.
• Some Muslims (e.g. women, the elderly, those with disabilities) may find it difficult to attend a mosque regularly. Their prayers at home are equally valid.
• What matters most is the intention (niyyah) behind the prayer, not the location. A sincere prayer at home is better than a distracted one in a mosque.
• In countries where Muslims are a minority, there may not be a nearby mosque.

Top band (10–12) Well-argued with developed points on both sides, religious references, justified conclusion.
Upper-mid band (7–9) Reasoned arguments on both sides with some development.
Lower-mid band (4–6) Arguments on one side or simple arguments on both sides.
Lower band (1–3) Simple statements or a single relevant point.

practice_questions.text: Explain two similarities between how Sunni and Shi’a Muslims observe Sawm during Ramadan.
practice_questions.marks:
Similarity 1: Both Sunni and Shi’a Muslims fast from dawn to sunset during Ramadan, abstaining from food, drink, smoking and sexual relations. Both see fasting as a compulsory pillar/obligatory act that demonstrates obedience to Allah. (2 marks)
Similarity 2: Both traditions recognise Laylat al-Qadr (the Night of Power) as a significant night in the last ten days of Ramadan. Both groups increase their worship during these nights, believing that worship on this night is ‘better than a thousand months’ (Qur’an 97:3). (2 marks)

before.content_html:
Zakah — Almsgiving

Zakah is the third pillar of Islam and means “purification” or “growth.” By giving away a portion of their wealth, Muslims purify what remains and acknowledge that all wealth ultimately belongs to Allah. It is not considered charity in the voluntary sense — it is a compulsory duty for every Muslim whose savings exceed a minimum threshold called the nisab.

Key Fact

Muslims must give 2.5% of their annual savings above the nisab threshold. The Qur’an specifies eight categories of people who may receive Zakah, including the poor, the needy, those in debt, and travellers in difficulty (Qur’an 9:60).

Origins and Purpose

Zakah has its origins in the Qur’an and the practice of the Prophet Muhammad. The Qur’an links prayer and charity repeatedly: “Establish prayer and pay Zakah” (Qur’an 2:43). This shows that worship of God and care for others are inseparable in Islam. The purpose of Zakah is threefold: it purifies the giver from greed and selfishness, it supports those in genuine need, and it reduces inequality within the ummah.

For the giver: Zakah purifies wealth by removing attachment to material possessions. It reminds Muslims that everything they own is a trust from Allah and develops generosity and compassion. Muslims believe that giving Zakah brings spiritual reward and protects them on the Day of Judgement.

For the recipient: Zakah provides essential support for the poor, the sick, travellers in need and those in debt. It helps prevent extreme poverty and ensures basic needs are met. The Qur’an identifies eight specific categories of recipient (9:60), ensuring money reaches those who need it most.

For the community: Zakah reduces the gap between rich and poor, creating a more just and equal society. It strengthens social bonds within the ummah because the wealthy are directly responsible for supporting the vulnerable. In some Muslim-majority countries, Zakah is collected and distributed by the state.

Khums means “one fifth” and is an additional financial duty unique to Shi’a Islam. Shi’a Muslims pay 20% of their surplus income (after living expenses) each year. Half of the Khums goes to Sayyids (descendants of the Prophet) and half to religious scholars and institutions. Khums is one of the Ten Obligatory Acts and reflects the Shi’a emphasis on supporting the Prophet’s family and the religious leadership.

Key Fact

Zakah (2.5% of savings) is paid by all Muslims, while Khums (20% of surplus income) is an additional duty for Shi’a Muslims. Both serve the purpose of social justice and redistributing wealth, but Khums also supports the Prophet’s descendants and Shi’a religious institutions.

Hajj — Pilgrimage to Makkah

Hajj is the fifth pillar of Islam. Every Muslim who is physically and financially able must make the pilgrimage to Makkah at least once in their lifetime. Hajj takes place during the Islamic month of Dhul Hijjah and attracts over two million Muslims from around the world each year. The Qur’an states: “Pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to God by people who are able to undertake it” (Qur’an 3:97).

Origins

Hajj traces its origins to the Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham). Muslims believe that Ibrahim and his son Isma’il built the Ka’aba as the first house of worship dedicated to the one true God. Many of the rituals performed during Hajj commemorate events from Ibrahim’s life — his willingness to sacrifice his son, his wife Hajar’s search for water, and his rejection of Satan’s temptations.

How Hajj is Performed

Hajj lasts five to six days and involves a series of rituals at sacred sites in and around Makkah. Before beginning, pilgrims enter a state of ihram — they wear simple white garments (two unstitched cloths for men), symbolising equality before God. All distinctions of wealth, status and nationality are stripped away.

Tawaf: Pilgrims walk around the Ka’aba seven times in an anti-clockwise direction. This represents the unity of Muslims in worshipping one God. The Ka’aba is believed to be directly below God’s throne in heaven.

Sa’i: Pilgrims walk seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwa, re-enacting Hajar’s desperate search for water for her son Isma’il. This commemorates God’s provision of the Zamzam well.

Arafat: Pilgrims travel to the plain of Arafat and stand in prayer and reflection from noon to sunset. This is considered the most important ritual of Hajj — the Prophet Muhammad said: “Hajj is Arafat.” It represents standing before God on the Day of Judgement.

Muzdalifah: After sunset at Arafat, pilgrims travel to Muzdalifah where they pray, rest under the open sky, and collect pebbles for the next day’s ritual.

Mina — Stoning the Pillars: At Mina, pilgrims throw pebbles at three stone pillars representing the places where Ibrahim rejected Satan’s temptations. This symbolises the Muslim’s rejection of evil and temptation in their own life.

Sacrifice: An animal (usually a sheep or goat) is sacrificed at Mina, commemorating Ibrahim’s willingness to sacrifice his son in obedience to God. The meat is distributed to the poor. This coincides with the festival of Id-ul-Adha celebrated by Muslims worldwide.

Key Fact

The key stages of Hajj include Tawaf (circling the Ka’aba), Sa’i (walking between Safa and Marwa), standing at Arafat, collecting pebbles at Muzdalifah, stoning the pillars at Mina, and animal sacrifice. Each ritual commemorates events from the life of Ibrahim and symbolises key aspects of Muslim faith.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the correct percentage of savings that Muslims must give as Zakah?
A) 1%
B) 2.5%
C) 5%
D) 10%
practice_questions.marks: B — 2.5% of annual savings above the nisab threshold. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Name two rituals performed during Hajj.
practice_questions.marks: Any two from: Tawaf (circling the Ka’aba) / Sa’i (walking between Safa and Marwa) / Standing at Arafat / Collecting pebbles at Muzdalifah / Stoning the pillars at Mina / Animal sacrifice. (1 mark for each, up to 2 marks)

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between Zakah in Sunni Islam and Khums in Shi’a Islam.
practice_questions.marks:
Difference 1: Zakah requires 2.5% of annual savings above the nisab threshold, while Khums requires 20% of surplus annual income after living expenses. Khums is therefore a significantly larger financial obligation. (2 marks)
Difference 2: Zakah is distributed to eight categories of need specified in the Qur’an (9:60), such as the poor and those in debt. Khums is split: half goes to Sayyids (descendants of the Prophet) and half to religious scholars and institutions. Khums therefore serves both social welfare and the Shi’a religious leadership. (2 marks)

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Hajj is important for Muslims. Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Reason 1: Hajj is a duty commanded by God — the Qur’an states ‘Pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to God by people who are able to undertake it’ (3:97). Fulfilling this obligation demonstrates complete submission to Allah’s will. (1–2 marks)
Reason 2: Hajj demonstrates the equality and unity of the ummah. All pilgrims wear simple white ihram garments, removing distinctions of wealth and status. Over two million Muslims from every nation stand together at Arafat, symbolising the Day of Judgement when all will stand equal before God. (1–2 marks)
Source: Muhammad said ‘Hajj is Arafat,’ showing that standing in prayer at Arafat is the most essential part of the pilgrimage. / Qur’an 3:97. (1–2 marks)

practice_questions.text:
‘Zakah is more important than Hajj because it helps other people.’
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Muslim teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments for:
• Zakah directly helps those in need — the poor, the sick, those in debt, and travellers. It addresses real-world suffering and social inequality.
• The Qur’an repeatedly links prayer and Zakah together (‘Establish prayer and pay Zakah’ — 2:43), showing that worship without social responsibility is incomplete.
• Zakah is annual and ongoing, while Hajj is a one-time obligation. Its cumulative impact on society is therefore greater.
• Helping others reflects Allah’s attribute of mercy and compassion.

Arguments against:
• Hajj is a direct command from God: ‘a duty owed to God by people who are able’ (Qur’an 3:97). Obeying God’s command is the highest priority for a Muslim.
• Hajj commemorates Ibrahim’s obedience and connects Muslims to the origins of their faith in a way Zakah cannot.
• Hajj is a transformative personal experience — standing at Arafat represents the Day of Judgement and inspires Muslims to live better lives afterwards.
• All five pillars are equally important because they form a complete framework for Islamic life. Removing any one weakens the whole.

Top band (10–12) Well-argued with developed points on both sides, religious references, justified conclusion.
Upper-mid band (7–9) Reasoned arguments on both sides with some development.
Lower-mid band (4–6) Arguments on one side or simple arguments on both sides.
Lower band (1–3) Simple statements or a single relevant point.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the rituals of Hajj connect Muslims to the Prophet Ibrahim.
practice_questions.marks:
Way 1: During Sa’i, pilgrims walk seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwa, re-enacting the journey of Ibrahim’s wife Hajar as she desperately searched for water for their son Isma’il. This commemorates God’s provision of the Zamzam well and Ibrahim’s trust in God. (2 marks)
Way 2: At Mina, pilgrims throw pebbles at three stone pillars, symbolising the places where Ibrahim rejected Satan’s attempts to persuade him not to sacrifice his son. This reminds Muslims to resist temptation and remain obedient to God, following Ibrahim’s example. (2 marks)

before.exam_tip_html: For jihad questions, always distinguish between greater jihad (inner spiritual struggle) and lesser jihad (physical/military struggle). Examiners specifically look for the conditions that must be met before lesser jihad can be declared — learn at least three with Qur’anic support (e.g. 2:190 and 8:61). For festivals, Ashura is the best topic for “Explain Similarities & Differences” questions because Sunni and Shi’a observances are completely different. Always reference the specific events each tradition commemorates.
before.content_html:
Jihad — Striving in the Way of God

The word jihad is one of the most misunderstood terms in Islam. It simply means “struggle” or “striving” and refers to the effort every Muslim must make to follow God’s path. Islam distinguishes between two forms of jihad: greater jihad and lesser jihad.

Greater Jihad — The Inner Struggle

Greater jihad is the daily personal battle every Muslim faces to live according to Allah’s will. It includes resisting temptation, overcoming selfishness, being honest, showing compassion, and striving to become a better person. The Prophet Muhammad is reported to have told soldiers returning from battle: “You have come from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad — the struggle of a person against their own desires” (Hadith). Scholars note that this hadith is graded as weak by Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, and it does not appear in the six authoritative collections (Kutub al-Sittah); it traces to al-Khatib al-Baghdadi's 11th-century History of Baghdad. Despite its uncertain chain of transmission, it remains widely quoted in discussions of jihad.

Key Fact

Greater jihad is considered more important than lesser jihad because it is a lifelong, continuous struggle. It includes studying the Qur’an, performing the Five Pillars, treating others justly, resisting greed and selfishness, and striving to improve oneself spiritually. Every Muslim engages in greater jihad every day.

Lesser Jihad — The Physical Struggle

Lesser jihad refers to the physical or military struggle to defend Islam when it is under threat. It is permitted only as a last resort and is subject to strict conditions. The Qur’an states: “Fight in God’s cause against those who fight you, but do not overstep the limits” (Qur’an 2:190). This verse makes clear that aggression and excess are forbidden.

Islamic teaching sets strict conditions that must be met before lesser jihad can be declared:

It must be defensive: Lesser jihad is only permitted to protect Islam, Muslim lands or oppressed people from attack. Aggressive warfare for conquest, territory or personal gain is forbidden.

It must be a last resort: All peaceful means of resolving the conflict — negotiation, diplomacy, treaties — must be exhausted first.

It must be declared by a recognised religious authority: No individual or group can declare jihad on their own. It requires the authority of a legitimate Muslim leader or scholar.

It must be proportionate: The Qur’an forbids excess (“do not overstep the limits” — 2:190). Civilians, women, children, the elderly, crops and livestock must not be targeted. Prisoners must be treated humanely.

It must stop when the enemy seeks peace: “If they incline towards peace, you must incline towards it too” (Qur’an 8:61).

Key Fact

Lesser jihad is only permitted when it is defensive, a last resort, declared by a legitimate authority, proportionate, and must cease when the enemy seeks peace. The Qur’an explicitly forbids aggression: “Fight in God’s cause against those who fight you, but do not overstep the limits” (2:190).

Both Sunni and Shi’a Muslims recognise greater and lesser jihad. However, jihad holds a particularly prominent place in Shi’a Islam as one of the Ten Obligatory Acts. Some Shi’a scholars have historically taught that only a divinely appointed Imam has the authority to declare lesser jihad, which in practice means it cannot be declared while the twelfth Imam remains in occultation. This view restricts the circumstances under which lesser jihad can occur. Other Shi’a scholars argue that senior religious leaders may authorise defensive action in the Imam’s absence.

Islamic Festivals and Commemorations

Festivals play an important role in Muslim life, bringing communities together in celebration and remembrance. The specification requires knowledge of three: Id-ul-Adha, Id-ul-Fitr, and Ashura.

Id-ul-Adha — The Festival of Sacrifice

Id-ul-Adha falls during the month of Dhul Hijjah and coincides with the Hajj pilgrimage. It commemorates the moment when Ibrahim was willing to sacrifice his son in obedience to God’s command. At the last moment, God provided a ram to sacrifice instead, showing that Ibrahim had passed the ultimate test of faith. Muslims around the world — not just those on Hajj — celebrate by sacrificing an animal (usually a sheep, goat or cow). The meat is divided into three portions: one for the family, one for friends and neighbours, and one for the poor.

Id-ul-Fitr — The Festival of Breaking the Fast

Id-ul-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan. After a month of fasting, prayer and self-reflection, Muslims celebrate with special prayers at the mosque, new clothes, festive meals, gifts and visiting family and friends. Before the Eid prayer, Muslims pay Zakat-ul-Fitr — a small charitable donation to ensure that even the poorest members of the community can join in the celebration. It is a day of gratitude to Allah for the strength to complete the fast and a time of joy shared with the whole community.

Ashura falls on the 10th day of Muharram, the first month of the Islamic calendar. Its meaning differs greatly between Sunni and Shi’a Muslims.

For Sunni Muslims, Ashura is a day of voluntary fasting. It commemorates the day when God saved the Prophet Musa (Moses) and the Israelites from the Pharaoh by parting the Red Sea. Muhammad fasted on this day and encouraged his followers to do the same.

For Shi’a Muslims, Ashura is the most solemn day of the year. It commemorates the martyrdom of Husayn, the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, who was killed at the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE. Husayn had refused to pledge allegiance to the Umayyad Caliph Yazid, whom Shi’a Muslims considered unjust and illegitimate. His death is seen as the ultimate sacrifice for justice and truth. Shi’a Muslims observe Ashura with mourning processions, dramatic re-enactments of the Battle of Karbala, and expressions of grief. It is a day of deep sorrow, not celebration.

Key Fact

Ashura shows the sharpest divide between Sunni and Shi’a practice. Sunni Muslims observe it as a day of fasting linked to Musa (Moses). Shi’a Muslims observe it as a day of intense mourning for Husayn’s martyrdom at Karbala in 680 CE — one of the most significant events in Shi’a history.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes ‘greater jihad’?
A) A military campaign to spread Islam
B) The personal struggle to live according to God’s will
C) A pilgrimage to a holy site
D) A festival celebrating the end of Ramadan
practice_questions.marks: B — The personal struggle to live according to God’s will. (1 mark)

practice_questions.text: Name two conditions that must be met before lesser jihad can be declared.
practice_questions.marks: Any two from: it must be defensive / it must be a last resort / it must be declared by a legitimate religious authority / it must be proportionate / it must stop when the enemy seeks peace. (1 mark for each, up to 2 marks)

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between how Sunni and Shi’a Muslims observe Ashura.
practice_questions.marks:
Difference 1: For Sunni Muslims, Ashura is a voluntary day of fasting. It commemorates the day God saved the Prophet Musa and the Israelites by parting the Red Sea. Muhammad fasted on this day and encouraged others to do so. (2 marks)
Difference 2: For Shi’a Muslims, Ashura is the most solemn day of the year — a day of intense mourning for the martyrdom of Husayn, the Prophet’s grandson, who was killed at the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE. Shi’a observe it with mourning processions and re-enactments, not fasting. (2 marks)

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Muslims believe greater jihad is more important than lesser jihad. Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Reason 1: Greater jihad is a lifelong, continuous struggle that every Muslim faces every day. It includes resisting temptation, studying the Qur’an, performing the Five Pillars, and striving to become a better person. Lesser jihad is only relevant in specific circumstances of conflict. (1–2 marks)
Reason 2: The Prophet Muhammad himself described the inner struggle as the ‘greater’ jihad. When soldiers returned from battle, he told them: ‘You have come from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad — the struggle of a person against their own desires.’ This shows that even the Prophet considered personal spiritual effort more important than military action. (1–2 marks)
Source: The Hadith about returning from lesser to greater jihad / The Qur’an states ‘Fight in God’s cause against those who fight you, but do not overstep the limits’ (2:190), showing lesser jihad is restricted while greater jihad is unlimited in scope. (1–2 marks)

practice_questions.text:
‘Islamic festivals are more important for building community than for personal faith.’
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Muslim teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments for:
• Id-ul-Fitr brings the whole community together after Ramadan with shared meals, gifts and prayers at the mosque. It strengthens bonds within the ummah.
• Id-ul-Adha involves sharing sacrificial meat with neighbours and the poor, directly building social connections and supporting those in need.
• Zakat-ul-Fitr ensures even the poorest can participate in Eid celebrations, showing festivals are designed to include the whole community.
• Shi’a mourning processions during Ashura are deeply communal events that reinforce shared identity and collective memory.

Arguments against:
• Id-ul-Adha commemorates Ibrahim’s personal obedience to God — the festival reminds every Muslim of the importance of individual submission to Allah.
• Ramadan and Id-ul-Fitr are fundamentally about each Muslim’s personal relationship with God through fasting, prayer and self-discipline.
• The Qur’an links festivals to worship and gratitude to God, not primarily to social bonding.
• Personal faith and community are inseparable in Islam — one strengthens the other. The Five Pillars themselves are both individual duties and communal practices.

Top band (10–12) Well-argued with developed points on both sides, religious references, justified conclusion.
Upper-mid band (7–9) Reasoned arguments on both sides with some development.
Lower-mid band (4–6) Arguments on one side or simple arguments on both sides.
Lower band (1–3) Simple statements or a single relevant point.

practice_questions.text: Explain two similarities between Id-ul-Adha and Id-ul-Fitr.
practice_questions.marks:
Similarity 1: Both festivals involve special communal prayers at the mosque, bringing the Muslim community together in shared worship. Both are joyful occasions that strengthen the sense of belonging to the ummah. (2 marks)
Similarity 2: Both festivals involve charity and sharing with the poor. During Id-ul-Adha, a third of the sacrificial meat is given to those in need. Before Id-ul-Fitr, Muslims pay Zakat-ul-Fitr to ensure the poorest can join the celebration. Both reflect the Islamic value of social justice. (2 marks)

flashcard_questions.q: An Arabic word meaning ‘struggle’ or ‘striving,’ referring to a Muslim’s effort to live according to God’s will.
The inner spiritual struggle to live as a good Muslim, resist temptation and follow God’s teachings — considered the most important form of jihad.
The physical or military struggle to defend Islam, permitted only under strict conditions as a last resort.
It simply means “struggle” or “striving” and refers to the effort every _____ must make to follow God’s path
_____ Jihad — The Physical Struggle Lesser jihad refers to the physical or military struggle to defend Islam when it is under threat

before.content_html:
Festivals and Commemorations in Islam

Muslims celebrate several important festivals throughout the year. You need to know three: Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha, and Ashura. Each festival has distinct origins, and Muslims celebrate them in different ways depending on their denomination.

Eid al-Fitr — The Festival of Breaking the Fast

Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan, the holy month of fasting. The word “Eid” means “festival” and “Fitr” means “breaking the fast.” It is a joyful celebration that thanks Allah for the strength to complete the fast and for the revelation of the Qur’an, which took place during Ramadan.

Key Fact

The Qur’an states: “He wants that you must complete the same number of days, and that you must magnify Allah for having guided you so that you may be grateful to Him” (2:185). This verse is primarily about the Ramadan fasting obligation and its concessions for the ill or travelling, ending with gratitude for divine guidance. Muslims connect the completion of Ramadan — mandated here — with the celebration of Eid al-Fitr.

Preparations begin before the day itself. Muslims send cards, decorate their homes, buy new clothes, and prepare special food and gifts. On the morning of Eid, Muslims rise early, bathe, and eat something sweet — traditionally dates — before attending the Eid prayer. The Prophet Muhammad himself consumed dates before the Eid prayer, and Muslims follow this Sunnah.

Before the Eid prayer, Muslims give Zakat al-Fitr — a small charitable donation (approximately £2–£5) so that poorer Muslims can also celebrate. The Eid prayer takes place at the mosque or in an open area such as a park. After the prayer, the Imam delivers a sermon. Muslims then exchange gifts, visit friends and family, and share a special meal together. It is also Sunnah to take a different route home from the one taken to the prayer. Many Muslims visit the cemetery to remember loved ones and forgive friends or relatives they have fallen out with.

In Muslim-majority countries, Eid al-Fitr is a public holiday. In the UK, British Muslims are often allowed a day off school or work. The festival reinforces the sense of ummah (community) as Muslims come together to celebrate after a month of shared spiritual discipline.

Eid al-Adha — The Festival of Sacrifice

Eid al-Adha takes place during the month of Dhul Hijjah and coincides with the annual Hajj pilgrimage. It commemorates the Prophet Ibrahim’s willingness to sacrifice his son when commanded by Allah. According to Islamic tradition, Ibrahim told his son of Allah’s command, and his son replied that they must do as Allah demanded. However, at the moment of sacrifice, Allah provided a ram to be killed instead. This demonstrated Ibrahim’s complete submission to the will of Allah.

Key Fact

The Qur’an teaches that Ibrahim agreed to sacrifice his son even though he was tempted by Shaytan (the devil). At three places, the angel Jibril told Ibrahim to “Pelt him,” so Ibrahim threw seven pebbles and Shaytan left. This event is re-enacted during Hajj at the Jamarat stone pillars.

The central act of Eid al-Adha is the Qurbani — the sacrifice of an animal, usually a sheep or goat. The meat is divided into three portions: one third for the family, one third for friends and neighbours, and one third distributed to the poor. This ensures that everyone, regardless of wealth, can share in the celebration.

Muslims also attend special Eid prayers at the mosque, listen to a sermon, wear their best clothes, and exchange gifts. For pilgrims on Hajj, this is a particularly solemn moment — men shave their heads and women cut a lock of hair, symbolising the end of the main pilgrimage rituals. The festival lasts for up to three days.

Ashura — A Day of Remembrance

Ashura falls on the 10th day of Muharram, the first month of the Islamic calendar. It is significant for both Sunni and Shi’a Muslims, but its origins and the way it is commemorated differ greatly between the two denominations. This makes Ashura one of the clearest examples of Sunni–Shi’a differences in practice.

Key Fact

For Shi’a Muslims, Ashura commemorates the martyrdom of Husayn, the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, at the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE. For Sunni Muslims, it recalls the day Allah saved Musa (Moses) and the Israelites from slavery in Egypt by parting the Red Sea.

After the death of the Prophet Muhammad, a dispute arose over who should lead the Muslim community. Shi’a Muslims believed leadership should stay within the Prophet’s family. In 680 CE, Yazid succeeded his father Muawiyah as Caliph. Yazid demanded that Husayn, Muhammad’s grandson and son of Imam Ali, pledge allegiance to him. Husayn refused because he believed Yazid was religiously misguided and that the agreement for leadership to remain within the Prophet’s family had been broken.

The people of Kufa invited Husayn to join them in opposition to Yazid. On his way to Kufa, Yazid’s army forced Husayn, his family, and a small group of supporters to stop at Karbala. They were denied water and food. After about seven days, Husayn and most of his family and companions were killed in battle. Husayn was beheaded. Shi’a Muslims regard Husayn and his followers as martyrs who chose death rather than compromise their beliefs.

Shi’a Muslims treat Ashura as an intense day of mourning and sorrow. Many wear black mourning clothes, participate in processions to mark the martyrdom, and listen to accounts and poems about Husayn’s death, which may lead to weeping. Some Shi’a Muslims make pilgrimage to Husayn’s shrine in Karbala (called Mashad al-Husayn). Some practise self-flagellation or give blood to remember the blood shed by the martyrs. Others pray and visit the mosque, reflecting on how a true Muslim should be steadfast in their faith as Husayn was.

Sunni Muslims commemorate Ashura primarily through voluntary fasting, following the example of the Prophet Muhammad, who fasted when he learned that the Jews of Medina fasted on this day to remember Allah saving Musa from the Egyptians. Sunni Muslims may also help the less fortunate, repent their sins, ask for forgiveness, and pray at the mosque. In Turkey, some eat a special pudding called Nuh’s pudding.

Ashura is sometimes debated as a term. Some argue it should not be called a “festival” or “celebration” at all, particularly for Shi’a Muslims, because the mood is one of grief and mourning rather than joy. This contrasts sharply with the celebratory atmosphere of Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha. Nevertheless, it remains one of the most significant dates in the Islamic calendar.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the festival that marks the end of Ramadan?
(a) Eid al-Adha
(b) Ashura
(c) Eid al-Fitr
(d) Jummah
practice_questions.marks: The correct answer is (c) Eid al-Fitr. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give one ways in which Muslims celebrate Eid al-Fitr.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for one correct point. Acceptable answers include:
Students may include:
• Attending the Eid prayer at the mosque or in an open area
• Giving Zakat al-Fitr (charitable donation) before the Eid prayer
• Wearing new or best clothes
• Sharing a special meal with family and friends
• Exchanging gifts and sending cards
• Eating dates or something sweet before the prayer
• Visiting the cemetery to remember loved ones
• Forgiving friends and relatives [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Explain two different ways in which Muslims commemorate the festival of Ashura.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include some of the following points:
• Shi’a Muslims treat Ashura as a day of intense mourning for the martyrdom of Husayn at the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE. They may wear black mourning clothes, participate in processions, listen to poems about Husayn’s death, or give blood to remember the martyrs.
• Sunni Muslims commemorate Ashura primarily through voluntary fasting, following the example of the Prophet Muhammad who fasted when he learned the Jews of Medina fasted to remember Allah saving Musa from the Egyptians.
• For Shi’a Muslims, the focus is grief and remembrance of injustice, while for Sunni Muslims, the focus is gratitude and devotion through fasting.
Award one mark for each brief/simple way identified, plus one development mark for each way explained. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which a Muslim celebrates Eid al-Adha. Refer to scripture or sacred writings in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Marking: First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks) = up to 6 marks.

Students may include some of the following points:
• Muslims perform Qurbani — the sacrifice of an animal (usually a sheep or goat). The meat is divided into three parts: one third for the family, one third for friends, and one third for the poor. This recalls Ibrahim’s willingness to sacrifice his son when Allah provided a ram instead.
• Muslims attend special Eid prayers at the mosque and listen to a sermon. They wear their best clothes and exchange gifts with family and friends.
• Reference to sacred writing, e.g. the Qur’an teaches that Ibrahim agreed to sacrifice his son even though he was tempted by Shaytan / ‘Ibrahim was tempted at three places but Jibril told him to pelt him’ (Hadith) / the story of Ibrahim’s complete submission to Allah.
• For pilgrims on Hajj, men shave their heads and women cut a lock of hair, symbolising the completion of the main pilgrimage rituals.
Award marks for identification, development, and relevant reference to scripture. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘Ashura is the most important out of all the Muslim festivals.’
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you:
• should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement
• should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• should refer to Muslim teaching
• may refer to non-religious arguments
• should reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Ashura is deeply significant for Shi’a Muslims as it commemorates the martyrdom of Husayn, the Prophet’s grandson, who chose death over compromising his faith at Karbala in 680 CE.
• The story of Husayn inspires Muslims to stand firm in their beliefs even in the face of injustice and oppression.
• For Sunni Muslims, Ashura also has prophetic significance as it recalls Allah saving Musa from the Egyptians.
Arguments against:
• Eid al-Fitr marks the completion of Ramadan (one of the Five Pillars) and is celebrated by all Muslims regardless of denomination.
• Eid al-Adha commemorates Ibrahim’s submission to Allah and coincides with Hajj (another Pillar), making it arguably more central to Islamic practice.
• Some Muslims argue all festivals are equally important as each reinforces different aspects of faith and obedience to Allah.
• Ashura is primarily significant for Shi’a Muslims; it holds less prominence for many Sunni Muslims who observe it through voluntary fasting rather than major commemoration.
Top band (10-12): A well-argued response with reasoned consideration of different points of view. Logical chains of reasoning leading to judgement(s) supported by knowledge and understanding. References to religion applied to the issue.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Reasoned consideration of different points of view with logical chains of reasoning. Clear reference to religion.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Reasoned consideration of a point of view with a logical chain of reasoning. OR Recognition of different points of view, each supported by relevant reasons. Maximum Level 2 if no reference to religion.
Lower band (1-3): Point of view with reason(s) stated in support.
0 marks: No relevant content.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which a Muslim celebrates Eid al-Fitr. Refer to scripture or sacred writings in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Marking: First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks) = up to 6 marks.

Students may include some of the following points:
• Muslims give Zakat al-Fitr before the Eid prayer (approximately £2–£5). This charitable donation was encouraged by the Prophet Muhammad and ensures the poor can also celebrate Eid.
• Muslims attend the Eid prayer in the mosque or an open area and listen to a sermon from the Imam. They exchange gifts and share a special meal to signify the end of Ramadan.
• Reference to scripture: ‘He wants that you must complete the same number of days, and that you must magnify Allah for having guided you so that you may be grateful to Him’ (Qur’an 2:185).
• ‘Verily it is only a festival for he whose fast Allah has accepted’ — this Hadith links the celebration directly to the successful completion of Sawm.
• Muslims rise early and bathe, following the Sunnah of the Prophet who bathed on the day of Fitr and Adha (Hadith).
Award marks for identification, development, and relevant reference to scripture. [6 marks]
